Where it began

Tony Greig was born in Queenstown, South Africa, on 6 October 1946. His father was a Scottish RAF officer, which is how Tony came to qualify for England. At Queen's College in his home town he was coached by a string of Sussex professionals who came out to work in the English winter, and every one of them noticed the tall, gifted boy.

After a first-class start with Border he went to Sussex for a trial at 19. He made 156 against Lancashire in his first game for the county and wrote home to say university would have to wait. His younger brother Ian later played Test cricket too.

The player

At six feet six inches, Greig was a fine sight at the crease and a versatile bowler, starting with medium pace and adding off-spin as his career went on. He played 58 Tests between 1972 and 1977, scoring 3,599 runs at 40.44 with 8 hundreds and taking 141 wickets at 32.21. He also held 77 catches.

His finest hour as a bowler came in the Caribbean in 1974. In the final Test in Trinidad he took 8 for 86 and 5 for 70, England won, and the series finished level. A few months later in Brisbane, with the Australian fast bowlers in full cry, he made 110 when almost everyone else was struggling.

What made him special

Greig loved a challenge and loved a crowd. Made England captain in 1975, he led his side in 14 Tests. The high point was the tour of India in 1976–77, when England won the first three Tests. He won over the vast Indian crowds, once falling down to play dead when a firecracker went off, and he rated his 103 at Calcutta, in front of 100,000 people, as the best moment of his cricket life.

One-day cricket should have suited him perfectly, yet in his 22 one-day internationals the big innings never quite arrived. It is about the only thing he left undone.

Away from the middle

After his playing days he settled in Australia and spent the rest of his life as a commentator for the Nine Network, much admired for being fair, funny and endlessly enthusiastic. He also broadcast for Channel Four, Sky and the SABC. Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year, and Sri Lankan fans took him to their hearts; in 2011 he became an ambassador for Sri Lanka Tourism, a country he never tired of praising on air.

And finally

Viewers of a certain age will remember his pitch reports, in which a car key or a pen was pushed into the surface to show how hard it was or how wide the cracks had grown. Once in a while the key went in and refused to come out, which told the audience everything they needed to know about the pitch.
